The acidity of a carboxylic acid is determined by the stability of its conjugate base. The more stable the conjugate base, the more acidic the acid. Electron-withdrawing groups (like chlorine) increase acidity by stabilizing the negative charge in the conjugate base.

The closer an electron-withdrawing group is to the carboxylic acid group, the stronger its effect on acidity. This is due to both inductive effects and field effects.

Looking at our options:
- Option A: CH3CH(Cl)CH2CO2H (3-chlorobutanoic acid) - Chlorine is 3 carbons away from the carboxyl group
- Option B: CH3CH2CH(Cl)CO2H (2-chlorobutanoic acid) - Chlorine is 2 carbons away from the carboxyl group
- Option C: CH3CH2CH2CO2H (butanoic acid) - No chlorine substituent
- Option D: ClCH2CH2CH2CO2H (4-chlorobutanoic acid) - Chlorine is 4 carbons away from the carboxyl group

Based on the principle that electron-withdrawing groups increase acidity and their effect decreases with distance, we can rank these as follows:

Option B (2-chlorobutanoic acid) would be most acidic because the chlorine is closest to the carboxyl group.
Option A (3-chlorobutanoic acid) would be next.
Option D (4-chlorobutanoic acid) would be slightly more acidic than butanoic acid.
Option C (butanoic acid) would be least acidic as it has no electron-withdrawing chlorine.

Therefore, the most acidic compound is option B: CH3CH2CH(Cl)CO2H (2-chlorobutanoic acid).
